summary: CodeShrink renders source code as images for a multimodal LLM and compresses them in three ways: removing layout whitespace with explicit structure markers (BFR), pruning instruction-irrelevant visual tokens (DTS), and a small Qwen3.5-0.8B policy trained with SFT and GRPO to choose a per-input resolution and pruning setting (ACC). On snippet-level tasks (300 Python code-QA, 200 clone-detection and 200 completion samples per language, Python and Java), a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen3.5-27B with CodeShrink matches or beats uncompressed text input while using 21-71% fewer visual tokens than a text-length-matched rendering.

claims.claim: CodeShrink reduces visual tokens by up to 71.2% while matching or exceeding uncompressed text-only input.
claims.evidence: 71.2% is Java clone detection in Table II (Acc 71.0 vs text-only 69.0). The ablation's full-system row for the same task (Table IV) reports R=53.5% and Acc 70.5, so the headline reduction is not reproduced within the paper. Other reductions: 39.7% (Python QA), 21.1% and 32.4% (completion). Single seed, greedy decoding, no CIs. Python QA 82.3 vs 81.0 is 4 of 300 questions.

claims.claim: CodeShrink consistently outperforms text-based and visual compression baselines.
claims.evidence: Tables I-II: e.g. Python QA 82.3 vs LongCodeZip 62.7, FastV 66.0, CodeOCR 51.7. But CodeShrink's downstream model is LoRA fine-tuned on in-task samples for OCR (§V-A3), and nothing indicates baselines received equivalent tuning. Without SFT, Python QA drops to 78.5 (Table IV), below text-only.

claims.claim: Blank-free rendering improves code-image reading across models without adaptation.
claims.evidence: Table III: Qwen3-VL, GPT-5-mini and Gemini-3-Flash at 1-8x, averaged over five runs. Mostly better, with large gains on completion and at high compression (GPT-5-mini QA at 8x: 52.5 -> 69.3), but GPT-5-mini is worse at low compression (QA 1x 76.4 -> 71.8; clone 2x 69.0 -> 65.7).

claims.claim: Per-sample adaptive configuration (ACC) is the most important component.
claims.evidence: Table IV: removing ACC lowers Python QA 81.5 -> 75.0 and Java clone 70.5 -> 64.5, and R roughly halves. The fixed configuration used for 'w/o ACC' is unspecified, and RQ4 shows per-task optima differ, so a per-task-tuned fixed setting (the obvious cheaper alternative) is not tested.

patterns.note: Compressing code input: text-token compressors (LLMLingua family, LongCodeZip) lose 18-21 points on Python code QA vs uncompressed text. Visual compression matches text only with task-specific LoRA fine-tuning of the reader model. Snippet-level inputs, single seed.
'Code QA' here is answering questions about a single given snippet (CodeOCR set), not repository-level exploration or onboarding questions.
A 0.8B policy trained with SFT and GRPO picks compression settings. It is compared only against an unspecified fixed configuration, not a per-task-tuned one.
Efficiency is reported as a visual-token reduction rate relative to text-length-matched rendering; no wall-clock or dollar cost, and the config-agent overhead is not counted.

methodology.sample: 300 Python code-QA (CodeOCR), 200 balanced Type-4 clone pairs (GPTCloneBench), 200 completion samples (LongCodeCompletion) per language; Java has no QA. Training uses 100 instances per task.
methodology.baselines: Text-only, no-context, LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, LongCodeZip, FastV, VisionZip, CodeOCR: current and relevant, but probably run without the task fine-tuning CodeShrink's reader receives.
methodology.models: Qwen3.5-27B reader (LoRA-tuned) and Qwen3.5-0.8B config agent for the main results; Qwen3-VL-235B, GPT-5-mini and Gemini-3-Flash for the rendering study only.
methodology.variance: Main and ablation results single seed (42), greedy decoding. Five-run averages only for Table III, with no spread shown.
methodology.ablations: Per-component (BFR, DTS, ACC, SFT) on Python and Java; configuration sweeps (Fig. 3).
methodology.contamination_controls: None. Public benchmarks such as GPTCloneBench and LongCodeCompletion may be in pretraining data.

biases.detail: Single seed for every main and ablation number; full-system numbers differ between Table II and Table IV (Java clone R 71.2 vs 53.5).
The reader model is fine-tuned on in-task samples while compression baselines and text-only appear to use an untuned model; the 'w/o ACC' fixed configuration is unspecified.
Snippet-level QA, clone and completion tasks; no repository-scale or agentic setting.
200-300 instances per task; differences of 1-2 points are a handful of items.
The full pipeline is evaluated on one reader model (Qwen3.5-27B).

verdict_reason: On-topic for LLM code understanding with current baselines, an ablation and released code. But all main results are single-seed, the abstract's 71.2% is not reproduced by the paper's own ablation row, the reader is task-fine-tuned while baselines likely are not, and the tasks are snippet-level.
applicability: Does not transfer to the team's discovery or onboarding harness. Agent hosts feed code as text through tools, and nothing here addresses repository-scale exploration of the Java ingestion services. The only usable signal is negative: generic text-token compressors (LLMLingua-style) badly degrade code question answering, so do not put such a compressor between the host and its code context to save tokens.
